raw_response:
I'm 63 this year, and I've been working this land in Quzhou for 45 years. I graduated from the agricultural technical school in Handan back in the 1980s, so I understand soil nutrient balances and crop water requirements better than most in my village. But understanding the science doesn't change the fact that I only have 10.1 mu and two people — my wife and me — to farm it. Our son works construction in Shijiazhuang. He sends a little money, but I never count on it. My decisions have to keep us fed and leave cash for doctor visits. At my age, a bad year is not something I can recover from.

This season, I've kept 7 mu in wheat-maize double cropping and 3.1 mu in cotton. I know the extension office pushes pure wheat-maize for efficiency, but I've always kept some cotton as a cash buffer. Old Wang down the road went all-in on wheat-maize last year and lost money when maize prices dropped in October. Diversification is my insurance.

For the winter wheat: I planted Jinmai 47 last October at 12.5 kg/mu. It came up evenly. Now it's early March. My target yield is 450 kg/mu — conservative, but realistic. I know from my training that the yield response curve to nitrogen flattens after 18 kg N/mu on these soils, and the marginal return isn't worth the risk for me. I'm applying 15 kg N/mu total: 8 kg as urea at green-up right now, and 7 kg at jointing in mid-April. I applied 6 kg P₂O₅ and 4 kg K₂O as base fertilizer last fall. For irrigation, I'll do three times — green-up, jointing, and grain filling — at about 40 yuan/mu each for electricity and water fees. The county extension recommends four irrigations for high yield, but I've calculated that the fourth irrigation only pays back if yield exceeds 520 kg/mu, which I'm not targeting. I'll spray a herbicide at green-up and a fungicide if I see powdery mildew at heading.

For summer maize: The turnaround after wheat harvest is always the bottleneck — sometimes only five to seven days. I don't own a no-till planter, so I hire a custom tractor to rotary till and plant immediately after the combine leaves the field. That costs me 50 yuan/mu but saves the crop. I'll plant Zhengdan 958, a hybrid I've used for ten years, at 2.5 kg/mu. Seed cost is 45 yuan/mu. For fertilizer, I'll band 10 kg N/mu and 3 kg P₂O₅/mu as compound fertilizer at planting, and if July rainfall is below 100 mm I'll side-dress another 4 kg N/mu in early August. I'll irrigate twice if needed — once at the six-leaf stage and once at tasseling. I expect 480 kg/mu.

For cotton: I plant in late April on the 3.1 mu with a local variety, using my own saved seed. Cotton is labor-intensive, which is why I limit it to 3.1 mu. I apply 12 kg N/mu — 5 kg at planting with phosphorus and potassium, and 7 kg at flowering in mid-July. I irrigate twice: at flowering and at boll formation. The real cost is picking. My wife and I can handle the September picks, but by October the volume is too much for our backs. I'll hire day laborers for about 4 days at 150 yuan/day. That's 600 yuan I have to reserve now. I target 260 kg/mu of seed cotton.

My total input budget this year is 5,800 yuan. That's almost everything I have in cash. I thought about pushing the wheat nitrogen to 18 kg/mu to try for 500 kg, but that extra 150 yuan in urea plus the irrigation cost is a gamble I can't afford at 63. If I get my 450 kg/mu of wheat and 480 kg/mu of maize, plus the cotton, we'll have enough to eat, pay the electric bills, and see the doctor if we need to. Stability is worth more than optimization when you have 10 mu.
